common_name: Basket of Fire Pepper (Texas Superstar Hanging-Basket Hot Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Basket of Fire is a Texas Superstar pepper bred specifically for hanging baskets and containers, with a naturally cascading habit and strong heat tolerance for Texas summers.

directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, large container, or garden bed in full sun. Basket of Fire is a Texas Superstar-designated ornamental-edible pepper bred for a compact, naturally trailing habit that shows off its abundant small, upright-then-cascading fruit especially well in a hanging basket, unlike most hot peppers, which grow upright. The fruit carries substantial heat, around 80,000 Scoville units, well into cayenne-and-above territory, ripening from green through yellow and orange to red, so a single plant often displays several fruit colors at once. It thrives in the heat and lower humidity of a Texas summer and continues producing heavily through the hottest months when many other peppers slow down. Harvest continuously to keep new fruit setting, and water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Purple Flash Pepper (Texas Superstar Variegated Ornamental Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Purple Flash is a Texas Superstar ornamental pepper grown primarily for its striking near-black, purple-and-white variegated foliage rather than for the fruit, and thrives in heat.

directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a container. Purple Flash is a Texas Superstar-designated ornamental pepper valued mainly as a striking foliage plant — its leaves are marbled in near-black purple, deep green, and creamy white, giving it a bold variegated presence unmatched by most other heat-loving bedding plants, and it holds this dramatic coloring through the hottest part of summer when many foliage plants fade. It does produce small, round, very hot purple-to-red fruit, but flowering and fruiting are secondary to its role as a colorful accent in mixed beds and containers. It performs best in full sun, where the foliage color intensifies, and tolerates heat and drought once established better than many variegated foliage plants. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier shape.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Ruby Crush Tomato (Texas Superstar Compact Disease-Resistant Grape Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Ruby Crush is a Texas Superstar determinate grape tomato bred with a broad disease resistance package, previously honored as a San Antonio Stock Show and Rodeo tomato before its Superstar designation.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Ruby Crush is a Texas Superstar-designated determinate grape tomato, compact enough for smaller garden beds and large containers, bred with a broad package of disease resistance that helps it hold up through the humid, disease-prone conditions of a Texas and Gulf South growing season. It produces heavy clusters of sweet, crack-resistant red grape tomatoes over a concentrated harvest window typical of determinate varieties, making it a good choice for gardeners who want a big, manageable crop for fresh eating or canning without the sprawling growth of an indeterminate vine. A light stake or cage helps keep the fruit-laden branches off the ground. Harvest regularly as fruit ripens to keep the plant productive through its season.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Balsamic Blooms Basil (Texas Superstar Edible-Flower Basil)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Balsamic Blooms is a Texas Superstar basil bred to keep producing tender, mild-flavored leaves and edible purple flowers together all season without the bitterness that normally develops in flowering basil.

directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Balsamic Blooms is a Texas Superstar-designated basil bred to solve a problem common to every other basil variety — once basil flowers, the leaves typically turn bitter and the plant's culinary usefulness declines — by keeping leaf flavor mild and pleasant even as it flowers continuously, so the whole plant, showy purple flower spikes included, stays harvestable and edible all season. This lets it double as both a productive culinary herb and an ornamental, pollinator-friendly bedding plant without the usual tradeoff of pinching off every flower to preserve leaf quality. Harvest leaves and flower spikes together for salads, garnishes, and infused vinegars. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier plant, though unlike most basil, letting it flower freely does not ruin its usefulness in the kitchen.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

planting.note: Plant small container-grown trees in fall or early spring in well-drained, alkaline, rocky or limestone soil in full sun; Lacey oak, a Texas Superstar tree, is slow-growing and best planted young, since it establishes more reliably as a smaller container tree than as a large balled-and-burlapped specimen.

directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline, rocky or limestone-derived soil in full sun; Lacey oak is a Texas Superstar-designated Hill Country native, valued for smoky blue-green summer foliage that emerges with an attractive soft pink flush in spring, along with excellent resistance to oak wilt, the vascular disease that has devastated live oaks and red oaks across parts of Texas. It grows slowly into a graceful, moderately sized shade tree well suited to the alkaline, rocky, drought-prone soils of the Texas Hill Country and similar limestone-based Gulf South sites where many other shade trees struggle. Its slow, controlled growth rate also means a naturally strong branch structure that needs relatively little corrective pruning compared to fast-growing trees. Once established, it is highly drought tolerant and needs no supplemental irrigation in most climates within its range. Give it plenty of room and full sun to develop its best form.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexican white oak, a Texas Superstar tree, grows considerably faster than most oaks and tolerates heat, wind, and drought better than many shade tree alternatives.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexican white oak, also called Monterrey oak, is a Texas Superstar-designated shade tree native to both a small area of south Texas and much of northeastern Mexico, prized for a faster growth rate than most oaks along with attractive peach-to-bronze new spring growth that matures to glossy green. It is semi-evergreen to evergreen in mild winters, dropping and replacing its leaves quickly in late winter rather than standing bare for long, and tolerates heat, wind, and drought impressively well once established, making it a strong, adaptable shade tree choice for difficult urban and suburban Texas and Gulf South sites. Its faster growth compared to slower native oaks makes it useful where a newly planted landscape needs shade sooner rather than decades later. Give it plenty of room to reach its substantial mature size, and provide regular water during the first couple of years to establish a deep root system before easing off to only occasional supplemental irrigation.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program
